facts.fact: In the claw grip, you curl your fingertips under and rest your knuckles against the flat side of the blade, so the knife edge meets your knuckles, not your fingertips.
facts.hook: a friend at a community kitchen keeps her fingers flat on the onion until a volunteer shows her the claw

facts.fact: Cutting an onion in half from top to root and laying each half flat side down gives a steady base, so the onion cannot roll while you slice it.
facts.hook: a whole onion keeps rolling off a wobbly camp table until someone halves it first

facts.fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
facts.hook: the cutting board skids every time a kid presses down at a friend's house

facts.fact: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it needs less pressure to cut, so it is less likely to slip off the food.
facts.hook: a kid pushes hard on a blunt knife and it skates off a tomato skin, so an adult swaps in a sharp one

facts.fact: When you cut an onion, broken cells release a sulfur gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide; it irritates the eyes, and the eyes make tears to wash it away.
facts.hook: two friends argue about whether onions are 'sad' while both of them are crying over the chopping board

facts.fact: Raw onion tastes sharp, but cooking it slowly over low heat makes it soft and sweet as its natural sugars turn golden brown.
facts.hook: a picky eater who hates raw onion tastes the slow-cooked ones and asks for more

facts.fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
facts.hook: the first batch of sauce tastes bitter because the garlic went in with the onions on high heat

facts.fact: In Italian cooking, soffritto is a base of finely chopped onion, carrot and celery cooked gently in olive oil before other ingredients go in.
facts.hook: a grandmother at the farmers' market insists every good sauce starts with three vegetables

facts.fact: Tomatoes came to Europe from the Americas; the earliest surviving printed tomato sauce recipes appear in Antonio Latini's cookbook published in Naples in 1692.
facts.hook: a kid claims Italians have made tomato sauce forever, and a cookbook at the community kitchen says otherwise

facts.fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
facts.hook: the sauce is too runny at dinnertime and someone realizes the lid has been on the whole time

facts.fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
facts.hook: a kid is about to pour all the pasta water down the drain when a friend saves a cupful

facts.fact: If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop; trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut.
facts.hook: a knife slides off the counter at a campsite and a kid's first instinct is to grab it

facts.fact: A monologue is a long speech by one character, spoken to other characters on stage or to the audience.
facts.hook: a kid at drama camp thinks a monologue means talking to yourself until the director explains

facts.fact: A soliloquy is a speech a character gives alone on stage, letting the audience hear the character's private thoughts.
facts.hook: at a community theatre a kid wonders who Hamlet is talking to when no one else is on stage

facts.fact: Hamlet's famous speech beginning 'To be, or not to be' is a soliloquy in Act 3, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's play.
facts.hook: a kid picks the most famous speech for an audition and has to find where it sits in the play

facts.fact: When Juliet asks 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' she means 'Why are you Romeo?', not 'Where are you?', because 'wherefore' means 'why'.
facts.hook: a kid performs Juliet's speech looking around the stage for Romeo, and a friend points out the mistake

facts.fact: Much of Shakespeare's verse is iambic pentameter: lines of ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed beat followed by a stressed one.
facts.hook: a kid rushes through a speech until a coach taps out the da-DUM rhythm on the table

facts.fact: The Russian director Konstantin Stanislavski co-founded the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898 and developed a system for acting truthful emotion on stage.
facts.hook: a drama camp teacher names the method behind asking 'what does your character want?'

facts.fact: In Stanislavski's system, an actor asks what the character wants in the scene, called the objective, and plays every line trying to get it.
facts.hook: a flat monologue comes alive once a kid decides what the character is trying to win

facts.fact: Actors split a script into beats: a new beat starts wherever a character's thought or tactic changes, and a pause often marks that shift.
facts.hook: a kid pencils slashes into a script to mark where to stop and breathe

facts.fact: The playwright Harold Pinter wrote 'Pause' and 'Silence' into his stage directions, treating silences as part of what the characters say.
facts.hook: a kid rehearsing at a grandparent's house finds a script where the pauses are written in like lines

facts.fact: Subtext is what a character means or feels beneath the words they actually say, and actors often show it through pauses, tone and gesture.
facts.hook: a character says 'I'm fine' and the kid has to make the audience know she isn't

facts.fact: Stage directions are given from the actor's view: stage left is the actor's left when facing the audience, and downstage means toward the audience.
facts.hook: a kid walks the wrong way on 'cross stage left' because he's thinking like the audience

facts.fact: Many old stages sloped upward away from the audience, which is why the back of the stage is still called upstage.
facts.hook: a kid at a community theatre wonders why the back is 'up' when the floor is flat

facts.fact: In Stephen Toulmin's model of argument, the claim is the point being argued, and the grounds or data are the evidence given to support it.
facts.hook: a debate partner keeps stating opinions until a coach asks for the evidence behind each one

facts.fact: The British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described his model of argument, including claim, data and warrant, in his 1958 book 'The Uses of Argument'.
facts.hook: a kid at a debate tournament asks where the word 'warrant' even comes from

facts.fact: A warrant explains why the evidence proves the claim; it is the logical link between them and is often left unstated by weaker debaters.
facts.hook: a judge says a team's facts were true but they never explained why the facts mattered

facts.fact: Toulmin's full model has six parts: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal.
facts.hook: a kid builds a case on index cards and realizes there are more boxes to fill than three

facts.fact: A qualifier is a word such as 'usually', 'most' or 'probably' that limits how strongly a claim is stated, making it harder to disprove.
facts.hook: an opponent knocks down 'all kids hate homework' with one counterexample

facts.fact: In his 'Rhetoric', Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, reasoning and evidence.
facts.hook: a debater relies only on a sad story and loses to a team with hard numbers

facts.fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is counted as a fallacy, a flaw in reasoning.
facts.hook: a debater says 'you're just a sixth grader' and the judge marks it down

facts.fact: A straw man argument misstates an opponent's position as something weaker or sillier, then attacks that version instead of the real one.
facts.hook: a team twists 'shorter recess' into 'no recess ever' and the other side calls it out

facts.fact: Two things happening together, a correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; a third factor may cause both.
facts.hook: a debater claims ice cream causes sunburn because both rise in summer

facts.fact: One personal story, called anecdotal evidence, cannot prove a general trend, because a single case may not be typical.
facts.hook: a team's whole case rests on what happened to one cousin

facts.fact: Lincoln-Douglas debate is named after the seven 1858 debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas during their race for a U.S. Senate seat in Illinois.
facts.hook: a kid entering a Lincoln-Douglas round asks who Douglas was

facts.fact: The side that proposes a change carries the burden of proof, meaning it must show why the change is needed rather than the other side proving it is not.
facts.hook: a team arguing for a new rule assumes the other side has to prove them wrong

facts.fact: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver.
facts.hook: a kid complains two minutes is too short to say anything important

facts.fact: People tend to remember the first and last items in a list best, a pattern called the serial position effect, which is why openings and closings matter.
facts.hook: a kid buries the best point in the middle and nobody remembers it

facts.fact: The psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus coined the term 'serial position effect' after memory experiments he performed on himself.
facts.hook: a kid researching speech tips finds a scientist who tested his own memory

facts.fact: Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.
facts.hook: a kid struggles to see why three points work better than seven

facts.fact: Repeating the same words at the start of several sentences is called anaphora; Martin Luther King Jr. repeated 'I have a dream' in his 1963 speech.
facts.hook: a kid wants a closing that sticks and borrows a repeated phrase

facts.fact: Martin Luther King Jr. gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech on August 28, 1963, at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
facts.hook: a kid choosing a model speech for a class assignment looks up where and when it was given

facts.fact: Glossophobia is the name for fear of public speaking, and it is one of the most commonly reported fears.
facts.hook: a kid's hands shake before the speech and a friend admits hers do too

facts.fact: A hook is the opening line that grabs attention, such as a question, a surprising fact or a very short story.
facts.hook: a kid opens with 'Today I will talk about...' and watches the audience drift off

facts.fact: Signposting words like 'first', 'second' and 'finally' tell listeners where they are in a speech, because they cannot flip back a page the way a reader can.
facts.hook: a grandparent loses track halfway through a practice speech

facts.fact: A short silent pause in place of 'um' or 'uh' makes a speaker sound more confident and gives listeners time to take in the point.
facts.hook: a friend counts every 'um' during a practice run

facts.fact: A callback closing returns to the opening hook at the end, which makes a speech feel complete.
facts.hook: a kid can't think how to end and realizes the answer is in the first line

facts.fact: Practicing a speech out loud with a timer matters because reading silently is faster than speaking, so a speech often runs longer than expected.
facts.hook: a speech that seemed short on paper runs well past the time limit at the first practice

facts.fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
facts.hook: a kid at drama camp keeps agreeing but never adds anything, and the scene stalls

facts.fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
facts.hook: a partner mimes holding a fishing rod and the kid doesn't notice it's an offer

facts.fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
facts.hook: a kid says 'no, that's not my dog' and the audience goes quiet

facts.fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
facts.hook: a kid freezes on stage until a partner calls her 'Captain'

facts.fact: Specific details, like 'Grandma's red bicycle' instead of 'a bike', give an improv partner more to build on.
facts.hook: a scene about 'some stuff' goes nowhere until one kid names exactly what it is

facts.fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
facts.hook: a drama camp counselor pulls out a worn book of games

facts.fact: Viola Spolin learned the use of games and play from Neva Boyd at Chicago's Hull House in the 1920s.
facts.hook: a kid learns that improv games began as games for children in a Chicago settlement house

facts.fact: The Second City, one of the most famous improv theaters, opened its first show in Chicago in December 1959.
facts.hook: a kid at a community theatre meets someone who trained in Chicago

facts.fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
facts.hook: a scene between a king and a servant gets funny when the servant starts giving orders

facts.fact: Keith Johnstone developed Theatresports in Calgary, Canada, a format where two teams of improvisers compete for audience or judges' approval.
facts.hook: a drama camp holds an improv match with teams and scores

facts.fact: Commedia dell'arte, which began in 16th-century Italy, was performed by masked actors who improvised dialogue around a plot outline.
facts.hook: a kid finds an old Harlequin mask in a theatre's costume room

facts.fact: The Harold, a long improvised form with linked scenes and callbacks, was developed by Del Close with the San Francisco group The Committee around 1967.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why a long-form improv show is named after a person called Harold

facts.fact: The Moon makes no light of its own; it shines only because it reflects sunlight.
facts.hook: at a planetarium a kid asks what the Moon burns to glow

facts.fact: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun; the phases show how much of that lit half faces Earth.
facts.hook: in the lamp-and-ball model, a kid sees the ball is always half lit even when it looks like a crescent

facts.fact: The phases are not caused by Earth's shadow; Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.
facts.hook: a friend insists the crescent is Earth's shadow until the lamp model shows otherwise

facts.fact: It takes about 29.5 days for the Moon to go from one new moon to the next.
facts.hook: a kid tracks the Moon on a calendar at a grandparent's house and counts the days

facts.fact: At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark.
facts.hook: a kid can't find the Moon at all one night and thinks it has vanished

facts.fact: At full moon, Earth lies roughly between the Sun and the Moon, so we see the whole lit side.
facts.hook: in the lamp model a kid has to hold the ball behind her own head without blocking the light

facts.fact: A waxing Moon's lit part is growing night by night, and a waning Moon's lit part is shrinking.
facts.hook: two cousins argue whether the Moon is getting bigger or smaller this week

facts.fact: A gibbous Moon is more than half lit but not yet full, while a crescent Moon is less than half lit.
facts.hook: a kid at a science museum doesn't know what to call the lumpy almost-full Moon

facts.fact: The Moon spins once for each trip around Earth, so the same side always faces us.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why the Moon's 'face' pattern never changes

facts.fact: The Moon rises on average about 50 minutes later each day, because it moves along its orbit while Earth turns.
facts.hook: a kid waiting to see moonrise at the same time as yesterday waits almost an hour

facts.fact: A waxing crescent is lit on the right side as seen from the Northern Hemisphere, but on the left side as seen from the Southern Hemisphere.
facts.hook: a video call with a cousin in Australia shows the Moon lit on the 'wrong' side

facts.fact: Around 1510, Leonardo da Vinci gave the earliest known explanation of the faint glow on a crescent Moon's dark part: sunlight reflected off Earth.
facts.hook: a kid notices the dark part of the crescent is not completely black

facts.fact: Erosion is the wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil; deposition is the dropping of that material somewhere else.
facts.hook: at a rock quarry a kid wonders where all the missing rock went

facts.fact: A river cuts downward mainly because the sand, pebbles and boulders it carries grind against its bed, a process called abrasion.
facts.hook: a kid finds a smooth, rounded stone and wonders what polished it

facts.fact: Faster water can carry bigger particles; when a river slows down, it drops its load, with the largest pieces settling first.
facts.hook: a stream table at the science museum leaves pebbles at the top and fine mud at the bottom

facts.fact: Scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago.
facts.hook: a kid at a grandparent's house looks at a Grand Canyon postcard and asks how long it took

facts.fact: The Grand Canyon is 277 miles (446 kilometers) long and over a mile deep at its deepest point.
facts.hook: a kid tries to picture a canyon deeper than a mile

facts.fact: In a canyon wall, harder rock layers tend to form steep cliffs and softer layers wear back into gentler slopes, which gives the Grand Canyon its stepped walls.
facts.hook: a kid at a rock quarry notices some layers stick out and others cave in

facts.fact: In layers of rock that have not been flipped or disturbed, the lowest layers are the oldest, an idea called the law of superposition.
facts.hook: a kid guesses the top layer of a canyon wall is the oldest

facts.fact: The Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older, in 1669.
facts.hook: a museum sign credits one scientist with reading rock layers like pages

facts.fact: The Scottish geologist James Hutton argued in 1785 that slow, everyday processes like erosion, working over immense time, shaped Earth's surface.
facts.hook: a kid can't believe a small river could ever cut a canyon

facts.fact: A delta forms where a river slows as it enters a sea or lake and drops the sediment it was carrying, building up new land.
facts.hook: a kid spots a fan of sand where a stream meets a pond

facts.fact: On a river bend, water flows fastest on the outside, eroding that bank, and slowest on the inside, where it deposits sand and gravel.
facts.hook: a kid notices a sandy beach on one side of a creek bend and a steep cut bank on the other

facts.fact: In 1869, John Wesley Powell led the first recorded expedition down the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon.
facts.hook: a museum exhibit shows a wooden boat and asks who went first

facts.fact: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens.
facts.hook: at a rock quarry a kid holds a speckled rock and asks if it was ever melted

facts.fact: Molten rock underground is called magma; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.
facts.hook: two friends argue whether a volcano spills magma or lava

facts.fact: Igneous rock that cools slowly underground, like granite, has large crystals, while rock that cools fast at the surface, like basalt, has tiny ones.
facts.hook: a kid compares a sparkly granite countertop with a plain dark basalt pebble

facts.fact: Obsidian is volcanic glass: lava that cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form.
facts.hook: a kid at a science museum thinks the shiny black rock is made of glass bottles

facts.fact: Pumice is an igneous rock full of gas bubbles trapped as lava cooled, and many pieces are light enough to float on water.
facts.hook: a kid drops a rock in a bucket at a grandparent's house and it doesn't sink

facts.fact: Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand, mud or shells are pressed together and cemented over time.
facts.hook: a kid sees stripes in a cliff at a quarry and asks why rock has layers

facts.fact: Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock usually destroys remains.
facts.hook: a kid searching for fossils keeps checking the wrong kind of rock

facts.fact: Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, so a drop of vinegar makes it fizz as carbon dioxide gas is released.
facts.hook: a kid tests quarry rocks with vinegar from a picnic basket

facts.fact: Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure deep underground without fully melting.
facts.hook: a kid assumes all rocks that were heated must have melted

facts.fact: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
facts.hook: a kid learns the marble statue at the museum started as seabed limestone

facts.fact: Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from shale, and it splits into thin flat sheets, which is why it has been used for roofs and chalkboards.
facts.hook: an old chalkboard at a grandparent's house turns out to be a rock

facts.fact: In the rock cycle, any type of rock can become any other type, through melting, weathering, or heat and pressure.
facts.hook: a kid thinks a rock stays the same kind forever

facts.fact: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
facts.hook: at a planetarium a kid notices the globe on display is leaning

facts.fact: Earth's axis points in the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and later leans away.
facts.hook: a kid walking a tilted globe around a lamp keeps turning it by mistake

facts.fact: In summer, sunlight strikes the ground more directly, so the same light is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more.
facts.hook: a flashlight pointed straight down makes a bright small circle, tilted it makes a dim wide one

facts.fact: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun also gets longer days, giving sunlight more hours to warm the ground.
facts.hook: a kid notices summer camp bedtime comes before dark

facts.fact: The noon Sun climbs higher in the sky in summer than in winter, so shadows at noon are shorter in summer.
facts.hook: a kid measures a fence post's noon shadow in June and December

facts.fact: Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer; around December 21, it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
facts.hook: a kid finds the two dotted lines on a globe and asks what they mark

facts.fact: At the equinoxes, around March 20 and September 22, day and night are roughly equal in length all over Earth.
facts.hook: a kid on a video call with a cousin across the world finds their sunsets match

facts.fact: North of the Arctic Circle, the Sun stays up for at least one full day around the June solstice, which is called the midnight sun.
facts.hook: a traveler's photo shows the Sun low in the sky at midnight

facts.fact: Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little and many places have wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones.
facts.hook: a friend from near the equator laughs at the idea of four seasons

facts.fact: The hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up.
facts.hook: a kid expects the longest day to be the hottest and it isn't

facts.fact: Earth's tilt slowly varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over a cycle of about 41,000 years.
facts.hook: a planetarium show asks what would happen if Earth leaned more

facts.fact: If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year, so there would be almost no seasons.
facts.hook: a kid holds the globe perfectly upright in the model and the seasons disappear

facts.fact: Interest is the price of borrowing money, usually charged as a percentage of the amount borrowed.
facts.hook: a kid at a bank asks why you pay back more than you borrowed

facts.fact: APR stands for annual percentage rate, the yearly interest rate a lender charges on money you borrow.
facts.hook: a kid reads 'APR' on a credit card ad at a grandparent's house

facts.fact: When unpaid interest is added to a debt, the next month's interest is charged on that interest too, so the debt grows faster over time.
facts.hook: a cousin's small balance keeps getting bigger even though she stopped using the card

facts.fact: Borrowing 100 dollars at 20 percent yearly interest and repaying it after one year costs about 20 dollars in interest, or more if interest compounds.
facts.hook: a kid wants a bike now instead of saving from lemonade stand earnings

facts.fact: Paying only the minimum on a credit card means much of each payment goes to interest, so paying off the balance can take years.
facts.hook: a relative explains why the card bill never seems to shrink

facts.fact: Many credit cards charge no interest on new purchases if the full statement balance is paid by the due date; this is called a grace period.
facts.hook: a kid learns her parent uses a card every week but never pays interest

facts.fact: Credit card interest rates are usually much higher than the interest a savings account pays you.
facts.hook: a kid at a bank compares the two rates on a brochure

facts.fact: The rule of 72 estimates how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate, so at 24 percent, about three years.
facts.hook: a kid calculates how fast an unpaid card debt could double

facts.fact: Cash advances from a credit card usually carry a higher interest rate than purchases, plus a fee, and interest often starts right away.
facts.hook: someone at a farmers' market pulls cash from a credit card and a friend warns her

facts.fact: In the United States, the classic FICO credit score runs from 300 to 850, and payment history is its biggest factor at about 35 percent.
facts.hook: a young adult at a bank learns why late payments matter later

facts.fact: Under the U.S. Credit CARD Act of 2009, people under 21 must show independent income or have a co-signer to get a credit card.
facts.hook: an older sibling tries to open a card at 19 and is asked about income

facts.fact: Diners Club, founded in 1950 in the United States, was the first independent payment card company, first used at restaurants.
facts.hook: a grandparent remembers when paying with a card was new
